title: Linux Operations Foundations
summary: Inspect a safe Linux sandbox using read-only and low-risk commands.
objectives: Use approved sandbox commands to inspect files, processes, and resource summaries.
Explain why students should observe and document before changing a system.

vocab.def: The organized way an operating system stores and names files.
An isolated environment for safe practice.

sections.heading: Operate in a sandbox
sections.body: A sandbox is separate from production systems. It lets students practice commands and record observations without accessing real infrastructure.

sections.heading: Safe inspection commands
sections.body: In the approved sandbox, commands such as pwd, ls, cd, cat, less, grep, head, tail, df, free, and ps can help inspect location, files, logs, storage, memory, and processes.

sections.heading: Observe before changing
sections.body: Do not use destructive deletion, privilege escalation, raw disk tools, shutdown commands, attack tools, or real network targets. Ask an instructor before changing the environment.

practice.prompt: In a simulated filesystem, identify the current directory, read a status file, and record one observation about storage or memory.

quiz.question: What is the safest first action when a sandbox system seems unusual?
options: Observe approved status information and document it
Delete files until it looks normal
quiz.answer: Observe approved status information and document it

lab.objective: Navigate an approved Linux sandbox with safe commands and complete an observation record.

reflectionPrompt: How does a sandbox change what is safe to try?
